idea.title: Make browser E2E safe by making the target impossible to confuse
idea.summary: A local browser E2E foundation used a disposable database, a strict target guard, deterministic seed data, and a file-backed test mailbox without changing production delivery behavior.

context.goal: Add reliable local browser coverage for authentication and password reset workflows.
context.situation: The application needed browser-level confidence without connecting tests to shared environments or real email delivery.
context.problem: An E2E runner can cause damage if its database target or delivery path is accidentally shared with development or production.
context.decision: Require E2E mode, a local host, and the exact disposable database name before setup; use a filesystem mailbox only in E2E mode.
context.implementation: Added target validation, deterministic seed data, disposable PostgreSQL lifecycle, isolated local storage, and two Playwright workflows.
context.result: A clean runner reset, migration, seed, API/web startup, and both browser workflows passed together against a local disposable database.

learning_points: Isolation should be enforced by executable checks, not naming conventions alone.
A fake external boundary can preserve the real user flow while keeping tests deterministic.
A full browser run is stronger evidence than unit tests for session and password-reset behavior.
story_points: The test database was treated as a safety boundary rather than merely a test fixture.
The password reset workflow reached a file mailbox instead of a mocked API response.
The final proof was a clean disposable environment running both user journeys together.
possible_angles: How to make E2E tests safer than your development database.
Why a file mailbox can be a better E2E test double than mocking email.
The difference between unit coverage and proving a real auth journey in a browser.

notes: No credentials, database URLs, or customer data captured.
